title: The Chance of At Least One
objective: After this level you can work out the chance of "at least one" by first finding the chance of none, as with a six in four rolls.
summary: An event and its opposite add up to 1, so "at least one" is 1 minus "none". No six in four rolls is 625/1,296 (about 48%), so at least one six is about 52%, as de Méré suspected.

cards.headline: A gambler in Pascal's day wondered about betting on a six in four rolls.
cards.body: The Chevalier de Méré, a French gambler, suspected it was a better bet than a similar one with two dice. Checking by listing every way four rolls can land would take all night. There's a far quicker route: work out the chance of the thing not happening.

cards.headline: Chance it happens = 1 minus chance it doesn't
cards.body: An event and its opposite cover everything that can happen, so their chances add up to 1. If a six has a chance of 1/6, no six has a chance of 5/6. That flip is the key to "at least one" questions. At least one six hides many cases: one six, two, three or four. No six at all is a single case, and Level 23's multiplying handles it.

cards.headline: De Méré's bet, solved
cards.body: No six on one roll: 5/6. No six in four independent rolls: 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6 × 5/6, which is 625 out of 1,296, about 48%. So at least one six comes up about 52% of the time. A small edge, but a real one. De Méré asked Pascal, whom you met in Level 1, whether this bet really beat a two-dice version, and Pascal proved his hunch right.

cards.fact: Double 6 in 24 rolls sounds as good. It falls just short.
cards.context: Try a second bet: at least one double 6 in 24 rolls of two dice. Same trick: no double 6 on one roll is 35/36, and multiplied 24 times it leaves at least one double 6 at about 49%. Just under even, and worse than the four-roll bet. Hunches get close; only the arithmetic tells which side of half you're on.

cards.headline: At least one: flipped
learned: A six in four rolls: about 52%

questions.prompt: The chance of at least one six in four rolls of a fair die is _____.

options.label: about 33%
options.rationale: Four rolls give more than a one-in-three chance.

options.label: about 48%
options.rationale: That is the chance of no six at all.

options.label: about 67%
options.rationale: That would come from adding 1/6 four times, which overcounts.

questions.explanation: No six in four rolls is 625/1,296, about 48%, so at least one six is about 52%.

questions.prompt: How does the shortcut find the chance of at least one six in four rolls?

options.label: Add 1/6 four times
options.rationale: Adding overcounts rolls with two or more sixes.

options.label: Find the chance of no six, then take it from 1
Multiply 1/6 by itself four times
options.rationale: That is the chance of four sixes, not at least one.

options.label: Divide 4 by 6
options.rationale: That treats each roll as adding a sixth, which overcounts.

questions.explanation: No six in four rolls is one case: 5/6 multiplied four times, about 48%. Take it from 1 and at least one six is about 52%.

questions.prompt: Using Level 23's multiplying, what is the chance of at least one head in three flips of a fair coin?

options.rationale: 1/8 is the chance of no head at all (three tails).
That is the chance of exactly one head; two or three heads count too.
Three flips give more than one chance at a head.

questions.explanation: No head in three flips means three tails: 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/8. So at least one head is 1 minus 1/8, or 7/8.
